course.title: CCNA Network Capstone
course.description: Run the network for a growing company: discover, design, build, prove, secure, operate and hand over a two-site network — the job, with CCNA technology inside it.
course.audience: Plan, build, operate and hand over a real two-site network as a four-person network team — starting from whatever equipment you actually have.

roles.name: Architecture
roles.mission: Owns the requirements, the design and the addressing plan. Reviews every change for design fit.
roles.label: 📐 Architecture

roles.name: Implementation
roles.mission: Owns switching, interfaces, wireless and the device build. Reviews the configuration itself.
roles.label: 🔌 Implementation

roles.name: Operations
roles.mission: Owns monitoring, backups, tickets and change records. Reviews the rollback on every change.
roles.label: 📡 Operations

roles.name: Automation & Security
roles.mission: Owns ACL policy, the management plane, Git and automation. Reviews the validation evidence.
roles.label: 🤖 Automation & Security

weeks.title: Acquisition & Kit
weeks.theme: What you have, and what it can do
weeks.objective: Declare how this build runs, register every device, and prove each capability with the command output that says so — because what your kit supports decides how every later week is built.

objectives.label: Register the kit and prove what it can do

weeks.milestone: The path is declared, every device is a row with its software version, and each capability is answered Yes or No with the output that proves it.

weeks.title: Connect
weeks.theme: Cable it, address it, reach it
weeks.objective: Discover what the business needs, design the shape of the network, then bring the first switches up: cabled, named, addressed, reachable, and documented.
weeks.milestone: Requirements and a high-level design are written, the first switches answer on the management VLAN, and every interface you touched is in the build log.

weeks.title: Segment
weeks.objective: Turn the flat office network into VLANs with trunks between switches, hand out addresses, and route between the departments the way your own kit allows.
weeks.milestone: Every department is its own VLAN, a trunk carries them between switches, a PC gets an address from DHCP, and the test matrix shows what reaches what.

weeks.title: Route
weeks.theme: A second building, and the internet
weeks.objective: Join the branch to headquarters, learn routes dynamically rather than by hand, and give the whole company one way out to the internet.

objectives.label: Give the site one way out to the internet

weeks.milestone: The two sites are adjacent, each learns the other’s networks without a static route, and a branch PC reaches the internet through one public address.

weeks.title: Protect
weeks.objective: Turn the policy into access lists, harden every device’s management plane, put the WLANs on the air, and prove the traffic that must NOT pass does not pass.

objectives.label: Turn the policy into access lists
Put the WLANs on the air

weeks.milestone: Guest cannot reach the LAN, only the network team reaches the management VLAN, every device takes SSH and refuses telnet, and the blocked tests are evidence.

weeks.title: Operate
weeks.theme: Run it, do not just build it
weeks.objective: Put the network under management: a source of truth in NetBox, configurations backed up and versioned, and every change requested, reviewed by a teammate and reversible.

objectives.label: Build a source of truth, not a spreadsheet
Back it up, then change it properly

weeks.milestone: NetBox holds the sites, devices, VLANs and prefixes; every configuration is backed up to Git; and one change has been through review, implementation and validation.

weeks.title: Observe
weeks.objective: Stand up a small NOC — polling, logs, latency and dashboards — then work a real ticket down the layers instead of guessing.

objectives.label: Work a ticket, not a hunch

weeks.milestone: Every device is polled and graphed, logs land in one place, latency is tracked, and a ticket has been worked from symptom to root cause with the evidence kept.

weeks.title: Automate
weeks.objective: Read the network through its APIs, describe it as data, and let Ansible configure from the source of truth rather than from your memory.

objectives.label: Configure from the source of truth

weeks.milestone: A playbook configures a VLAN on every access switch from data held in NetBox, and running it twice changes nothing the second time.

weeks.title: Engineer
weeks.theme: Something breaks. Then you hand it over.
weeks.objective: Work an injected failure as an incident, find the root cause, fix it under change control, prove the fix, and hand the network to whoever runs it next.
weeks.milestone: The incident is documented from ticket to prevention, the fix went through a reviewed change, and the as-built handover would let a stranger run this network on Monday.

tasks.title: Decide how this build runs
tasks.objective: Choose emulated or physical, get the tool or the cable working, and reach a device prompt — the one thing Week 1 cannot start without.
learn: What emulation can and cannot teach
definitionOfDone: The path is recorded in the Kit & Capability Register
A device prompt is open in front of you
The machine you work from is named in the register

steps.title: Pick the path, and know what it costs you
steps.description: The team has agreed one path and the reason, and it is written in the register.
steps.where: Anywhere — this is a team decision
steps.instruction: Decide as a team: Emulated or Physical kit. Emulation gives you every device the design calls for; hardware gives you cabling, optics, PoE and real interface counters. Both are first-class here — record which one you are on.
steps.expectedOutput: The team has agreed one path and the reason, and it is written in the register.
instructionList: Emulated: Every device the design calls for, free, and you can break it without consequence.
Emulated — the limit: No cabling, no optics, no PoE, no interface errors — Week 1 records those as design decisions rather than doing them.
Physical kit: Cabling, optics, PoE, console recovery and the interface counters that only real copper produces.
Physical kit — the limit: Costs money, and what your specific models support decides how some weeks are built — which is what the register is for.
steps.whatItMeans: Neither path is the lesser one. Emulation cannot teach you what a bad patch lead feels like; hardware cannot give you eight routers on a laptop.

steps.title: Get to a prompt
steps.description: A device prompt is in front of you and Enter produces another prompt rather than nothing.
steps.where: Your own machine — emulator or console cable
steps.instruction: Open the emulator and place one switch, or plug the console cable into a real one and open your terminal program. You are done when a device prompt answers you.
steps.expectedOutput: A device prompt is in front of you and Enter produces another prompt rather than nothing.

fixes.symptom: No prompt over the console cable?
fixes.fix: Check the speed is 9600 8N1 and that you picked the right COM port — the cable’s driver renames it on every machine.

fixes.symptom: The emulator will not start the device?
fixes.fix: It is almost always memory. Close everything else, or start with one switch rather than the whole topology.

steps.whatItMeans: Everything else in this course assumes you can type at a device. Prove it now, not in Week 1 when something else is also broken.

tasks.title: Register the kit and prove what it can do
tasks.objective: One row per device with its real software version, then each capability answered Yes or No with the command output that proves it — the document every later week reads.
prerequisites: A device prompt, from the previous task
definitionOfDone: Every device is a row: name, what it is, model, software version, ports
At least eight capabilities answered Yes or No
Every Yes carries the line of output that proves it
The gaps are written down, with what you will do instead

handoff.note: Which procedure Week 2 takes — SVIs or router-on-a-stick — is decided by this register.

steps.title: Read what the device really is
steps.description: The model and the image, from the device rather than the sticker.
steps.instruction: Run these on every device you have and copy the answers into the register. The sticker tells you what was sold; the image decides what it can do.

commands.explain: Model, software version and feature set. The version is why a feature is missing.
commands.sample:
Cisco IOS Software, C2960X Software (C2960X-UNIVERSALK9-M), Version 15.2(7)E3
Model number: WS-C2960X-24TS-L
System image file is "flash:/c2960x-universalk9-mz.152-7.E3.bin"

commands.explain: Every port, its speed, and whether an SFP uplink exists. This is your usable port count.
commands.sample:
Port      Name     Status       Vlan    Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/1            connected    1       a-full  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/25           notconnect   1         auto   auto unknown  (SFP)

steps.whatItMeans: Two switches with the same model number can differ by one licence line. The register records what is in front of you.
steps.expectedOutput:
Switch# show version
Cisco IOS Software, C2960X Software (C2960X-UNIVERSALK9-M), Version 15.2(7)E3
Model number: WS-C2960X-24TS-L

Switch# show interfaces status
Port      Name     Status       Vlan    Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/1            connected    1       a-full  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/25           notconnect   1         auto   auto unknown  (SFP)

outputHighlights.label: The image — this is what decides which features exist.
An SFP uplink port. Present but unpopulated still counts as fibre-capable.

steps.title: Prove each capability, one command at a time
steps.description: Yes or No, with the line that says so.
steps.instruction: Work down the capability list in the register. Run the command, read the tell, record the answer, and paste the line. A "Yes" with no output beside it is an opinion.
instructionList: Console access (blue cable or USB) — run `show users`: the line marked `*` is `con 0` — you are on the console
VLANs — run `show vlan brief`: VLAN 1 is listed, so the table exists and can be added to
802.1Q trunking — run `show interfaces trunk`: the command exists and prints a table, even an empty one
Inter-VLAN routing on the switch (SVI) — run `show ip route`: a routing table is printed rather than "Invalid input"
EtherChannel / LACP — run `show etherchannel summary`: the command is recognised — protocol column appears
OSPF — run `show ip protocols`: OSPF appears, or `router ospf 1` is accepted in config mode

commands.explain: The single most useful question: can this switch route at all? A table means yes.
commands.sample:
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.50.99.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan99

commands.explain: Whether two links can be bonded. Recognised at all is the pass; groups come later.
commands.sample:
Number of channel-groups in use: 0
Number of aggregators:           0

commands.explain: PoE budget per port — what the phones and the access point will run on.

steps.whatItMeans: An "Invalid input detected" is a real answer: it means No, and it tells you which alternate procedure your build takes.
steps.expectedOutput: Every capability row has Yes or No, the device it was tested on, and a line of output. Some will be No — that is information, not failure.

fixes.symptom: "Invalid input detected" on a show command?
fixes.fix: That is your No. Record it, and read what the course does instead — every capability has an alternative.

fixes.symptom: The command works but the table is empty?
fixes.fix: Empty is a pass. You are asking whether the device CAN, not whether it already does.

steps.title: Write down the gaps, and what one purchase would unlock
steps.description: The gaps section names every No and its alternative, and the next purchase is a capability rather than a sh…
steps.instruction: One line per No: what you will do instead. Then, if you were buying one thing, what and why — capability first, model second.
steps.expectedOutput: The gaps section names every No and its alternative, and the next purchase is a capability rather than a shopping list.
steps.whatItMeans: This paragraph is the one Week 2 and Week 4 follow. A team that wrote it honestly never hits a wall mid-build.

tasks.title: Discover before you design
tasks.objective: Interview the business and survey the building: who needs what, what cannot go down, and what is already there.
definitionOfDone: Three or more departments recorded with what they need
The availability requirement is written in the business’s own words
The survey says what exists today and what is wrong with it

steps.title: Ask the business what it needs
steps.description: The requirements form names every department, its people and its needs — and one sentence on what downtime…
steps.where: With your instructor, or from the scenario
steps.instruction: Northgate Supply Co.: One flat network, one switch out of ports, and a second building opening in six weeks. Record the departments, what each one does on the network, and what cannot go down.
steps.expectedOutput: The requirements form names every department, its people and its needs — and one sentence on what downtime costs.
steps.whatItMeans: A requirement you did not write down is a requirement somebody will dispute in Week 8.

steps.title: Walk the building
steps.description: The survey records the rooms, the drops, the cable runs and the ISP handoff.
steps.where: Both sites — on foot, or from the site notes
steps.instruction: Record where the equipment lives, how many drops there are, and where the circuit comes in. MDF in the server room, one IDF on the warehouse mezzanine; the branch has one wall-mount cabinet in the office.
steps.expectedOutput: The survey records the rooms, the drops, the cable runs and the ISP handoff.
steps.whatItMeans: The building decides half the design: cable distance, where power is, and where a switch can actually live.

tasks.title: Design the shape
tasks.objective: Turn the requirements into a high-level design: the sites, the link between them, where routing happens, and which boundaries exist.
prerequisites: The Kit & Capability Register — it decides what you can design
definitionOfDone: Four or more decisions, each traced to a requirement
Each decision says what was rejected and why
Each decision says whether your kit supports it

steps.title: Decide where routing happens
steps.description: The design states where inter-VLAN routing happens and which capability answer made that the choice.
steps.instruction: If the register says you have a switch that routes, the core routes between VLANs. If it does not, the router does, over one trunk. Write the decision down with the reason.
steps.expectedOutput: The design states where inter-VLAN routing happens and which capability answer made that the choice.
steps.whatItMeans: This is the decision your Week-0 register already made for you. Writing it down is what makes it reviewable.

steps.title: Name the boundaries
steps.description: Every boundary is a sentence a manager would agree with, and Week 4 turns each one into an access list.
steps.instruction: Say what must not reach what — guest from corporate, users from management, cameras from servers — in the business’s words, before any ACL exists.
steps.expectedOutput: Every boundary is a sentence a manager would agree with, and Week 4 turns each one into an access list.
steps.whatItMeans: A boundary stated in business words survives a change of staff. One stated as an ACL number does not.

tasks.title: Bring the first switches up
tasks.objective: Cable, name, address and reach the first switches: a management address, a working uplink, and an interface list that matches the plan.
definitionOfDone: Each switch answers on the MGMT VLAN
Every interface you touched is in the build log with what proved it
The configuration is saved on every device

steps.title: Name it, address it, save it
steps.description: Each switch answers a ping on its management address, and `show running-config` survives a reload.
steps.instruction: Set the hostname from the plan, give the switch its management address in MGMT, and save. A device you cannot reach is a device you will be walking to all term.
steps.expectedOutput: Each switch answers a ping on its management address, and `show running-config` survives a reload.
steps.whatItMeans: A switch you cannot reach remotely is a switch you will be walking to for the rest of the course.

steps.title: Read the interfaces like an engineer
steps.description: Interface status matches the plan, and the error counters are clean on every link you rely on.
steps.instruction: Check every port you cabled: up, the speed you expected, no errors climbing. A link that is up at 100 Mbps when you expected 1 Gbps is a cable problem you want to find now.
steps.expectedOutput: Interface status matches the plan, and the error counters are clean on every link you rely on.
steps.whatItMeans: Interface counters are the only place a bad cable admits what it is doing. Read them before you trust the link.

tasks.title: Cut the network into departments
tasks.objective: Create the VLANs from the plan, put the access ports in them, and trunk the switches together so one cable carries all of it.
definitionOfDone: Every VLAN in the plan exists on every switch that needs it
The trunk carries them, with the native VLAN stated
A PC in one VLAN cannot see a PC in another — yet

steps.title: Write the plan down before you configure it
steps.description: The LLD holds every VLAN with its prefix and gateway, and every port range is assigned.
steps.instruction: One row per VLAN: id, name, purpose, prefix, gateway, DHCP range. Then the ports. Configuring first and documenting later is how the two end up different.
steps.expectedOutput: The LLD holds every VLAN with its prefix and gateway, and every port range is assigned.
steps.whatItMeans: Configure first and document later, and the two end up different — usually on the port nobody checked.

steps.title: Create the VLANs and trunk the switches
steps.description: The VLAN table matches the plan on every switch, and the trunk shows the expected VLAN list on both sides.
steps.instruction: Create each VLAN, put the access ports where the plan says, then make the switch-to-switch link a trunk and state the native VLAN explicitly on both ends.
steps.expectedOutput: The VLAN table matches the plan on every switch, and the trunk shows the expected VLAN list on both sides.
steps.whatItMeans: A native VLAN that differs on the two ends of a trunk is the classic fault. Stating it explicitly is the fix.

tasks.title: Route between the departments
tasks.objective: Give every VLAN a gateway and let the departments reach each other — on the switch if your kit routes, on a router over one trunk if it does not.
prerequisites: The Kit & Capability Register — it decides which of the two procedures you follow
definitionOfDone: Every VLAN has a gateway that answers a ping
A PC in one VLAN reaches a server in another
The route table shows one connected route per VLAN

steps.title: Give every VLAN a gateway
steps.description: Each gateway address answers a ping from a host in its own VLAN.
steps.where: The routing device — your core switch or your router
steps.instruction: Your register decided this: an SVI per VLAN on a switch that routes, or a subinterface per VLAN on a router over one trunk. Same outcome, different device.
steps.expectedOutput: Each gateway address answers a ping from a host in its own VLAN.
steps.whatItMeans: Same requirement, two procedures. Which one you follow was decided in Week 0 by what your kit can do.

steps.title: Hand out addresses, then prove it end to end
steps.description: A client gets an address from the right pool with the right gateway, and reaches a host in another VLAN.
steps.where: The DHCP device, then a client
steps.instruction: Serve DHCP where the plan says — on the network device or relayed to the server — then release and renew on a client and watch it get the right address, mask and gateway.
steps.expectedOutput: A client gets an address from the right pool with the right gateway, and reaches a host in another VLAN.
steps.whatItMeans: DHCP is where a design meets a real client. A wrong gateway in the pool looks exactly like a routing fault.

tasks.title: Survive a cable being pulled
tasks.objective: Add a second link between switches and prove the network keeps working when one of them dies — bonded if your kit does EtherChannel, blocked by spanning tree if not.
definitionOfDone: A second link exists between two switches
You know which link is forwarding and which is not
Pulling one link is a test row with a measured recovery

steps.title: Decide where the root of the tree should be
steps.description: The core is the root bridge, on purpose, and you can show the command that says so.
steps.instruction: Spanning tree picks a root for you, and its choice is usually wrong — the oldest switch wins. Set it deliberately to the core and record why.
steps.expectedOutput: The core is the root bridge, on purpose, and you can show the command that says so.
steps.whatItMeans: Spanning tree always picks a root. Left alone it picks the oldest switch in the building, which is rarely where you want it.

steps.title: Pull the cable and time it
steps.description: The test matrix has a row with the measured number of lost pings, and traffic recovered without anyone touc…
steps.instruction: Start a continuous ping across the link, pull the forwarding cable, and count the lost replies before it recovers. That number is your failover time.
steps.expectedOutput: The test matrix has a row with the measured number of lost pings, and traffic recovered without anyone touching a keyboard.
steps.whatItMeans: Redundancy nobody has tested is a belief. The number of lost pings is the evidence.

tasks.title: Join the second building
tasks.objective: Address the link between the sites, bring up the adjacency, and let each site learn the other's networks without a single static route.
definitionOfDone: The two routers are OSPF neighbours in the FULL state
Each site learns the other’s prefixes as OSPF routes
A branch PC reaches an HQ server by address

steps.title: Address the link between the buildings
steps.description: Each router pings the other across the WAN link, and both interfaces are up.
steps.instruction: A point-to-point link needs exactly two addresses, which is why the plan uses a 30-bit mask. Configure both ends and prove they ping each other before you add any protocol.
steps.expectedOutput: Each router pings the other across the WAN link, and both interfaces are up.
steps.whatItMeans: Prove the link before you add a protocol on top of it, or you will be debugging two things at once.

steps.title: Turn OSPF on, then read the adjacency
steps.description: The neighbour table shows FULL, and each router has routes it did not have before, marked as OSPF.
steps.instruction: Advertise the networks into OSPF area 0 on both sides, then check the neighbour state. A neighbour stuck below FULL is telling you something specific — read it rather than restarting the process.
steps.expectedOutput: The neighbour table shows FULL, and each router has routes it did not have before, marked as OSPF.
steps.whatItMeans: A neighbour stuck below FULL names its own problem — mismatched masks, timers or areas. Read the state.

steps.title: Prove it the way a user would
steps.description: A trace from a branch PC to an HQ server crosses the WAN in the expected number of hops.
steps.instruction: Ping and trace from an actual branch client to an actual HQ server. The route table being right is not the same as the user being able to work.
steps.expectedOutput: A trace from a branch PC to an HQ server crosses the WAN in the expected number of hops.
steps.whatItMeans: A correct route table is not the same as a user who can work. Test from where the user sits.

tasks.title: One way out to the internet
tasks.objective: Point a default route at the ISP, translate the whole company behind one public address, and prove both sites get out.
definitionOfDone: A default route points at the ISP and is learned by the branch too
Inside addresses are translated to one outside address
A client at each site resolves a name and reaches the internet

steps.title: Default route out, and share it
steps.description: The branch router shows a default route learned from OSPF, not typed in locally.
steps.instruction: Point a default route at the ISP gateway, then advertise it so the branch learns the way out too rather than having its own hard-coded copy.
steps.expectedOutput: The branch router shows a default route learned from OSPF, not typed in locally.
steps.whatItMeans: One default route, advertised once, beats a copy on every device that somebody has to remember to change.

steps.title: Translate the inside to the outside
steps.description: The translation table shows real sessions, and a client at each site reaches the internet by name.
steps.instruction: Mark the inside and outside interfaces, translate the internal ranges to the outside address, and then watch the translation table fill as a client browses.
steps.expectedOutput: The translation table shows real sessions, and a client at each site reaches the internet by name.
steps.whatItMeans: The translation table is where NAT stops being theory: you can watch a session appear as somebody browses.

tasks.title: Turn the policy into access lists
tasks.objective: Write each business rule as an ACL, apply it in the right place and direction, and prove both what passes and what does not.
definitionOfDone: Every rule in the policy has an ACL and a place it is applied
Guest cannot reach the LAN, proven by a test that fails on purpose
No ACL exists that you cannot trace to a business rule

steps.title: Write the rule before the ACL
steps.description: Every row has a rule, an ACL name, and the interface and direction it is applied to.
steps.instruction: One row per rule, in the words the business would use, then the ACL name. An ACL nobody can trace to a rule is one nobody dares change later.
steps.expectedOutput: Every row has a rule, an ACL name, and the interface and direction it is applied to.
steps.whatItMeans: An ACL nobody can trace to a business rule is an ACL nobody dares touch two years from now.

steps.title: Apply it, then try to break it
steps.description: The test matrix has blocked rows that are blocked, and allowed rows that still work.
steps.where: The routing device, then a client in each VLAN
steps.instruction: Apply each ACL, then test from the guest VLAN into the LAN and from the user VLAN into management. The tests that must FAIL are the evidence that the policy works.
steps.expectedOutput: The test matrix has blocked rows that are blocked, and allowed rows that still work.
steps.whatItMeans: The tests that must FAIL are the segmentation evidence. Everything else only proves the network works.

tasks.title: Harden the management plane
tasks.objective: Make the devices themselves defensible: SSH instead of telnet, real secrets, unused ports shut, and port security where a stranger could plug in.
definitionOfDone: Every device takes SSH and refuses telnet
Unused access ports are shut or protected
All devices agree on the time

steps.title: Close the front door
steps.description: SSH connects, telnet is refused, and the banner appears before the login prompt.
steps.instruction: Generate keys, enable SSH, disable telnet on the lines, set a real enable secret, and put a banner up. Then prove telnet fails — an untested claim is not a control.
steps.expectedOutput: SSH connects, telnet is refused, and the banner appears before the login prompt.
steps.whatItMeans: Telnet sends the password in clear text on the management VLAN — the one network you least want read.

steps.title: Make the logs agree about time
steps.description: Every device reports synchronised time from the same source.
steps.instruction: Point every device at the same time source. Without it, correlating a switch log with a router log during an incident is guesswork.
steps.expectedOutput: Every device reports synchronised time from the same source.
steps.whatItMeans: Without synchronised clocks, correlating a switch log with a router log during an incident is guesswork.

tasks.title: Put the WLANs on the air
tasks.objective: Map the corporate, guest and IOT SSIDs onto their VLANs so wireless inherits exactly the segmentation the wired network already has.
prerequisites: An access point, or the emulator’s wireless model — the register says which
definitionOfDone: Each SSID lands in its own VLAN
A guest client gets a guest address and cannot reach the LAN
The AP uplink carries exactly the VLANs the WLANs need

steps.title: One SSID per VLAN, and no surprises
steps.description: Each SSID is on the air and a client on it gets an address from that VLAN’s pool.
steps.instruction: Create a WLAN per group — corporate, guest, IOT — and map each to its VLAN. Guest on the air must be as isolated as guest on copper, and the GUEST rules already say so.
steps.expectedOutput: Each SSID is on the air and a client on it gets an address from that VLAN’s pool.
steps.whatItMeans: Wireless is not a separate network. An SSID is a VLAN with an aerial, and it inherits that VLAN’s rules.

steps.title: Test wireless like a visitor would
steps.description: The test matrix shows guest-to-LAN blocked from wireless as well as wired.
steps.instruction: Join the guest SSID and try to reach a server. It must fail, for the same reason and by the same ACL as it fails on copper.
steps.expectedOutput: The test matrix shows guest-to-LAN blocked from wireless as well as wired.
steps.whatItMeans: A guest who is isolated on copper and free on wireless is not isolated. Test the air as well.

tasks.title: A source of truth, not a spreadsheet
tasks.objective: Load the sites, devices, VLANs and prefixes into NetBox so the documentation becomes a system other tools can read.
definitionOfDone: Both sites, every device and every prefix exist in NetBox
The VLAN list in NetBox matches the LLD exactly
You can answer "what is in 10.50.20.0/24" without opening a switch

steps.title: Model what you already documented
steps.description: NetBox answers the same questions your LLD does, and disagrees with it nowhere.
steps.instruction: Create the sites, then the devices, then the prefixes and VLANs — in that order, because each one hangs off the last. Your LLD is the input.
steps.expectedOutput: NetBox answers the same questions your LLD does, and disagrees with it nowhere.
steps.whatItMeans: A spreadsheet answers questions you ask. A source of truth answers questions your tools ask.

tasks.title: Back it up, then change it properly
tasks.objective: Get every configuration into version control, then run one real change through request, peer review, backup, implementation and validation.
definitionOfDone: Every device’s configuration is backed up automatically
One restore has actually been proven, not assumed
One change has been reviewed by a teammate before it was made

handoff.note: The reviewer checks the addressing and the design fit before the change is made.

steps.title: Collect every configuration, automatically
steps.description: Every device appears in the repository, and a second run shows a diff only where something really changed.
steps.instruction: Point Oxidized at the devices and let it pull their configurations into Git. A backup somebody has to remember to take is not a backup.
steps.expectedOutput: Every device appears in the repository, and a second run shows a diff only where something really changed.
steps.whatItMeans: A backup somebody has to remember to take is not a backup. Automate the collection, then prove a restore.

steps.title: Run one change the way a business would
steps.description: The change record is complete, a teammate’s name is on the review, and the validation tests were re-run aft…
steps.where: The change record, then the device
steps.instruction: Raise it, write the rollback FIRST, get a teammate to review it, back up, implement, re-run the validation tests, and record the result — including if it failed.
steps.expectedOutput: The change record is complete, a teammate’s name is on the review, and the validation tests were re-run afterwards.
steps.whatItMeans: Writing the rollback first is the test of whether you understand the change. If you cannot, you are not ready.

tasks.title: Build a small NOC
tasks.objective: Poll every device, centralise the logs, watch the latency, and put it on one screen you would actually look at.
definitionOfDone: Every device is polled and graphed
Logs from every device land in one place
Six things are monitored, each with a threshold and an owner

steps.title: Poll the devices and graph what matters
steps.description: Every device is green in the monitoring system and its uplink graph is drawing.
steps.where: The tools host, then each device
steps.instruction: Enable read-only SNMP on the kit, add them to LibreNMS, and check that interface, CPU and memory graphs start filling. Then set the thresholds that would actually page somebody.
steps.expectedOutput: Every device is green in the monitoring system and its uplink graph is drawing.
steps.whatItMeans: Monitoring exists so the network tells you before a user does. A threshold nobody would act on is noise.

steps.title: Send every log to one place
steps.description: Shutting a port produces a log line at the collector, with time that matches the device.
steps.instruction: Point syslog at the collector and prove it: make something happen — shut an interface — and watch the line arrive with the right timestamp.
steps.expectedOutput: Shutting a port produces a log line at the collector, with time that matches the device.
steps.whatItMeans: Logs in one place with the right time turn "it broke this morning" into a sequence you can read.

tasks.title: Work a ticket, not a hunch
tasks.objective: Take a user-reported symptom and isolate it by layer, recording what you ruled out as carefully as what you found.
definitionOfDone: The scope is established before any device is touched
Each layer you ruled out is recorded with how
The root cause names a cause, not a symptom

steps.title: Establish the scope before you touch anything
steps.description: The ticket states who is affected, since when, and what changed recently.
steps.instruction: One user or twenty? One VLAN or all of them? Since when, and what changed? Five minutes here saves an hour of poking at the wrong device.
steps.expectedOutput: The ticket states who is affected, since when, and what changed recently.
steps.whatItMeans: Five minutes establishing scope saves an hour of poking at the wrong device.

steps.title: Work down the layers, and capture the proof
steps.description: The log records each layer ruled out and how, and the root cause is a cause rather than a restatement of th…
steps.where: The devices, and a capture where needed
steps.instruction: Layer 1, then 2, then 3, then the services. Where the answer is not obvious, capture the traffic and read what actually happens rather than what should.
steps.expectedOutput: The log records each layer ruled out and how, and the root cause is a cause rather than a restatement of the symptom.
steps.whatItMeans: What you ruled out is as much of the record as what you found — it is how the next person trusts your conclusion.

tasks.title: The network as data
tasks.objective: Read the network through an API instead of a screen, and describe intent as YAML rather than as remembered commands.
definitionOfDone: You can pull the device list out of NetBox with one request
The intended VLAN list exists as YAML, not just in a config
You can explain what idempotent means with your own example

steps.title: Ask the source of truth a question
steps.description: A single request returns your device list as JSON, and you can pick out one field from it.
steps.instruction: Query the NetBox API for your devices and read the JSON that comes back. This is the same data the dashboard shows, in the form a script can use.
steps.expectedOutput: A single request returns your device list as JSON, and you can pick out one field from it.
steps.whatItMeans: The same data the dashboard draws, in the form a script can use. That is all an API is.

tasks.title: Configure from the source of truth
tasks.objective: Write a playbook that adds a VLAN to every access switch from the data in NetBox — and that does nothing at all the second time you run it.
definitionOfDone: A playbook configures the same VLAN on every access switch
Running it twice reports no changes the second time
The change went through the same review as a manual one

steps.title: One playbook, every switch
steps.description: The second run reports zero changes, which is what "idempotent" means when you can see it.
steps.instruction: Build the inventory from NetBox, write the playbook, run it against one switch, then all of them. Then run it again and watch it change nothing.
steps.expectedOutput: The second run reports zero changes, which is what "idempotent" means when you can see it.
steps.whatItMeans: Idempotent means running it again is safe. The second run changing nothing is how you see it.

steps.title: Automation is still a change
steps.description: The automated change has a change record with a reviewer and re-run validation tests.
steps.instruction: A playbook that touches eight switches is a bigger change than one that touches one. It goes through the same request, review and validation as anything else.
steps.expectedOutput: The automated change has a change record with a reviewer and re-run validation tests.
steps.whatItMeans: Automation multiplies a mistake across every device. That makes review more important, not less.

tasks.title: Something breaks — work it properly
tasks.objective: Your instructor breaks something. Find it as an incident, fix it under change control, prove the fix, and write the root cause and the prevention.
definitionOfDone: The incident is timed: reported, understood, fixed
The root cause is a cause, and the fix is under a change record
A preventive action is named that is a check or a standard, not "be careful"

steps.title: Triage, then isolate
steps.description: The log shows the scope, the timeline, and each layer ruled out on the way to the cause.
steps.instruction: Establish scope and impact first, check what changed, then work the layers. Your monitoring should tell you something before any user does.
steps.expectedOutput: The log shows the scope, the timeline, and each layer ruled out on the way to the cause.
steps.whatItMeans: Your monitoring should have told you first. If a user did, that is a finding about the monitoring.

steps.title: Fix it under change control, then prevent it
steps.description: The fix is recorded as a change, the validation tests pass again, and the preventive action is something a…
steps.where: The change record, then the device
steps.instruction: Even in an incident: the fix is a change, with a rollback. Then write what stops it happening again — a pre-change check, a template, a standard.
steps.expectedOutput: The fix is recorded as a change, the validation tests pass again, and the preventive action is something a team could actually follow.
steps.whatItMeans: An incident is not an excuse to skip change control. It is when a rollback matters most.

tasks.title: Hand the network over

A first-day health runbook exists, ten minutes long
No passwords appear in the document

steps.description: Every difference between the design and the build is stated with why it happened.
steps.instruction: Compare the as-built to the HLD and LLD, and write down every difference with the reason. Most will trace to a line in your Week-0 capability register.
steps.expectedOutput: Every difference between the design and the build is stated with why it happened.
steps.whatItMeans: Where the build differs from the design is the most interesting page in the document, not the embarrassing one.

steps.title: Write the first-day runbook

steps.instruction: Ten minutes, in order: what to look at, what good looks like, and one test that must fail. If a stranger cannot follow it, it is not a runbook.
steps.expectedOutput: A stranger could confirm this network is healthy in ten minutes using only your runbook.
steps.whatItMeans: A runbook a stranger cannot follow is a note to yourself. Ten minutes, in order, no assumed knowledge.

deliverables.title: Kit & Capability Register
deliverables.purpose: What equipment the team has, what each device can actually do, and which of the two paths — emulated or physical — this build runs on. Every later week reads this: what your kit supports decides how you build, so this is recorded before anything is designed.
deliverables.howTo: Declare the path. List every device you own, borrowed, plan to buy, or will emulate. Then answer each capability Yes or No — and paste the command output that proves it, because a datasheet describes the model that was sold, not the switch in front of you.
buildSteps: Declare the path first: emulated or physical. It changes nothing about the design and everything about how you build it.
One row per device. Read the model and software version off `show version` rather than the sticker — the sticker lies about the image.
Count the access ports you can actually use, and note whether the uplinks are copper or SFP.
For each capability, run the command in the "How to prove it" column and record Yes or No.
Paste the line that proves it into the evidence column. "Yes" with no evidence is an opinion.
Name the machine you work from — it belongs in the topology documentation like any other host.
Read the gaps: every No tells you which alternate procedure your build takes, and what buying one thing would unlock.
deliverables.meaning: A good register lets somebody else pick up your kit and know, without touching it, what this network can be asked to do. The gaps matter more than the strengths: a No against "switch that routes" is not a failure, it is the reason your Week-2 procedure is router-on-a-stick.
deliverables.useIt: Week 1 designs against it, Week 2 branches on it, and the buying guide beside it says what one more purchase would unlock. It is also the first appendix of the handover package.
pitfalls: Claiming a capability from the datasheet. The image on the device decides, and only `show` output proves it.
Leaving "to buy" rows out. A gap you have not written down is a gap you discover mid-build.
Recording the workstation in detail. It matters only as far as it runs the emulator and appears in the documentation — the kit is the subject here.

deliverables.title: Requirements & Site Survey
deliverables.purpose: What the business needs the network to do, and what is physically there today. Written before any design, because a design nobody traced to a requirement is a preference.
deliverables.howTo: Interview the business (your instructor plays it, or use the scenario). Record what each department needs, what cannot go down, and what exists in the building already.
buildSteps: Count the people, per department, and what each group actually does on the network.
List the applications that matter and who needs them.
Ask what cannot go down, and for how long — that is your availability requirement.
Walk the building: where the cabinet is, how many drops, where the cable runs, where the ISP comes in.
Record the constraints honestly — budget, existing kit, cabling, the ISP circuit.
Write down the problems the business already has. Those are the requirements nobody will state directly.
deliverables.meaning: Every later decision points back to a line here. If you cannot name the requirement a VLAN serves, the VLAN is decoration.
deliverables.useIt: The High-Level Design is built from it, and the handover opens with it.

CAPABILITIES.label: Console access (blue cable or USB)
CAPABILITIES.what: Reach a device with no configuration at all, and recover one you have locked yourself out of.

proof.tell: the line marked `*` is `con 0` — you are on the console

CAPABILITIES.without: In an emulator the console IS the terminal the tool opens for you.

CAPABILITIES.label: VLANs
CAPABILITIES.what: Split one physical switch into separate networks — the whole of Week 2.

proof.tell: VLAN 1 is listed, so the table exists and can be added to

CAPABILITIES.without: An unmanaged switch cannot do this at all — this is the one capability the course genuinely requires, on hardware or in an emulator.

CAPABILITIES.label: 802.1Q trunking
CAPABILITIES.what: Carry several VLANs down one cable between switches.

proof.tell: the command exists and prints a table, even an empty one

CAPABILITIES.without: One cable per VLAN between switches — it works, it does not scale, and saying why is the lesson.

CAPABILITIES.label: Inter-VLAN routing on the switch (SVI)
CAPABILITIES.what: Route between VLANs in the switch itself, at wire speed.

proof.tell: a routing table is printed rather than "Invalid input"

CAPABILITIES.without: Router-on-a-stick: one trunk to a router, a subinterface per VLAN. Slower, and the CCNA outcome is the same.

CAPABILITIES.label: EtherChannel / LACP
CAPABILITIES.what: Bond two links into one, so a cable can fail without an outage.

proof.tell: the command is recognised — protocol column appears

CAPABILITIES.without: Two links and spanning tree: one forwards, one blocks. You still prove redundancy, with a slower failover.

CAPABILITIES.label: OSPF
CAPABILITIES.what: Learn routes dynamically between the two buildings — the whole of Week 3.

proof.tell: OSPF appears, or `router ospf 1` is accepted in config mode

CAPABILITIES.without: Static routes both ways, then a deliberate failure to show what static routing cannot do for you.

CAPABILITIES.label: NAT / PAT
CAPABILITIES.what: Let the whole company reach the internet through one public address.

proof.tell: the command is recognised (an empty table is a pass)

CAPABILITIES.without: The emulator provides the internet edge; the design is documented and the configuration is written even when nothing upstream answers.

CAPABILITIES.label: Access control lists
CAPABILITIES.what: Turn the business rules into what the network will and will not carry.
CAPABILITIES.without: Nothing: every managed device in this course can do ACLs. If yours cannot, it is unmanaged.

CAPABILITIES.label: Power over Ethernet
CAPABILITIES.what: Power the phones and the access point from the switch port.
CAPABILITIES.without: A PoE injector for the AP, and the phones are documented as a design requirement rather than built.

CAPABILITIES.label: Fibre uplink (SFP)
CAPABILITIES.what: Uplink between rooms further apart than copper will carry.

proof.tell: an SFP or Te/Gi uplink port appears, even unpopulated

CAPABILITIES.without: Copper uplinks, with the distance limit recorded in the site survey as the reason fibre would be needed.

CAPABILITIES.label: An access point
CAPABILITIES.what: Put the corporate, guest and IOT WLANs on the air.

proof.tell: on a controller: the AP is listed and joined

CAPABILITIES.without: The WLANs are configured in the emulator and the VLAN-to-SSID mapping is documented.

CAPABILITIES.label: A wireless controller
CAPABILITIES.what: Run several APs as one system, with WLANs defined once.
CAPABILITIES.without: A standalone AP, or Mobility Express on the AP itself. The WLAN-to-VLAN design does not change.

CAPABILITIES.label: DHCP served by the network device
CAPABILITIES.what: Hand out addresses without a server — the usual small-site answer.
CAPABILITIES.without: The server VM serves DHCP and the router relays with `ip helper-address` — which is the enterprise pattern anyway.

CAPABILITIES.label: SSH to the device
CAPABILITIES.what: Administer the kit without sending the password in clear text.

proof.tell: SSH is Enabled, with a version

CAPABILITIES.without: Telnet on the management VLAN only, documented as a risk with the remediation named. An image without crypto cannot do SSH.

CAPABILITIES.label: SNMP
CAPABILITIES.what: Let the monitoring system read interfaces, CPU and memory.

proof.tell: the command is recognised — chassis and contact appear

CAPABILITIES.without: Syslog and reachability checks only. You still build the NOC; it sees less.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).

glossary.data.src_ip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a network (Suricata) alert — who the traffic came from.
glossary.data.srcip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a host alert (logins, web requests). Its network twin is data.src_ip — search both.
glossary.ossec.conf: The Wazuh agent's config file. It names the SOC to report to and any extra log files to ship.
glossary.hydra: A password-guessing tool. In this lab you run it against your own pod so the SOC has a brute-force attack to detect.
glossary.tcpdump: A command-line tool that records network traffic to a .pcap file you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.Wireshark: A traffic viewer. Open a .pcap in it and "Follow HTTP Stream" to read the exact request an attacker sent.
glossary.Kali: The attacker machine in your lab — a Linux build that ships with nmap, nikto, hydra and the rest.
glossary.Proxmox: A hypervisor — an operating system whose job is to run virtual machines. In Server+ you install it on your own server; in the CySA lab it already runs the lab.
glossary.POST: Power-On Self-Test — the hardware check a machine runs the moment you power it on, before any operating system. Beeps and blink codes are POST talking to you.
glossary.DIMM: A memory stick. Which slots they go in is dictated by the motherboard manual, and the wrong slots can stop the machine starting at all.
glossary.ECC: Error-Correcting Code memory — server RAM that detects and fixes single-bit corruption on the fly. Servers use it; desktops usually do not.
glossary.HCL: Hardware Compatibility List — the check that the software you plan to run officially supports the exact hardware you have, before you build on it.
glossary.UEFI: The modern replacement for the old BIOS firmware. Boot mode matters: an OS installed under UEFI will not boot if the firmware is later switched to legacy.
glossary.IOMMU: The chip feature (Intel VT-d / AMD-Vi) that lets a virtual machine be handed a real piece of hardware, like a NIC, as its own.
glossary.VT-x: Intel’s virtualization extensions. Present is not enough — they must be ENABLED in firmware setup, or the hypervisor cannot start a single VM.
glossary.stripe size: How large a chunk of data a RAID array writes to one disk before moving to the next. The default is right for this build.
glossary.IDS: Intrusion Detection System — software that watches traffic and raises an alert when it matches a known attack pattern. Suricata is yours.
glossary.NVD: National Vulnerability Database — the public catalogue you search to find a CVE and its score for a given software version.
glossary.pod: Your team’s pair of machines: one Ubuntu web server and one Windows PC.
glossary.escalate: Pass an alert on for deeper investigation, with the reason written down, instead of closing it yourself.
glossary.SOC: Security Operations Centre — the team (and dashboard) that watches for attacks around the clock.
glossary.SIEM: Security Information and Event Management — software that gathers logs from everywhere and raises alerts. Wazuh is your SIEM.
glossary.IOC: Indicator of Compromise — a clue an attacker leaves behind, like a bad IP address, file name, or hash.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public ID for one specific known software flaw, e.g. CVE-2021-41773.
glossary.CVSS: A 0–10 score for how severe a vulnerability is, so you can rank what to fix first.
glossary.pcap: A 'packet capture' — a saved recording of network traffic you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.SQLi: SQL injection — tricking a website into running database commands it shouldn't, often to steal data.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall — a filter in front of a website that blocks common attacks like SQL injection.
glossary.POA&M: Plan of Action & Milestones — a to-do list for fixing findings: what, who owns it, and by when.
glossary.PTES: Penetration Testing Execution Standard — the agreed steps of a pentest: recon, scan, exploit, report.
glossary.STRIDE: A checklist of threat types: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
glossary.NIC: Network Interface Card — a machine's network connection. On these VMs it's usually named ens18.
glossary.IaC: Infrastructure as Code — describing machines in a text file a tool applies, so the build is repeatable and the file is the record. Terraform or OpenTofu is yours.
glossary.OpenTofu: The open-source fork of Terraform, kept under the Linux Foundation after HashiCorp changed Terraform’s licence in 2023. Same HCL, same providers, same state files; the command is tofu instead of terraform.
glossary.exporter: A small program on a host that publishes its metrics on an HTTP port for Prometheus to collect. node_exporter for Linux, windows_exporter for Windows.
glossary.IPAM: IP Address Management — the tool that holds every subnet and address and who has it, so the plan and reality are the same document. NetBox is yours.
glossary.FIM: File Integrity Monitoring — an agent that hashes important files and alerts when one changes, which is how a tampered config gets noticed.
glossary.cloud-init: The first-boot setup a cloud image runs: hostname, user, keys and addressing handed in from outside, so a clone comes up configured instead of blank.
glossary.DNAT: Destination NAT — the host rewriting where a packet is going. The rule that turns a request to the host’s campus address on port 80 into a request to websrv in the DMZ.
glossary.MASQUERADE: Source NAT behind the host’s own address, so a reply from the campus LAN or the internet comes back to the host and is handed to the guest that asked.
glossary.published port: A port on the host’s campus address that a DNAT rule hands to a VM behind it. Each one is a deliberate hole in the segmentation, and you should be able to say why it exists.
glossary.idempotent: Running it twice gives the same result as running it once. The property that makes a playbook safe to run every night — and why changed=0 on the second run is the proof.
glossary.drift: Reality diverging from what the code says — a change made in the console instead of the repository. terraform plan (tofu plan) detects it; the next apply may undo it.
glossary.dynamic inventory: Ansible asking the hypervisor which hosts exist instead of reading a list someone typed. The list is never out of date because there is no list.
glossary.XDR: Extended Detection and Response — one platform watching endpoints, logs and files across a whole fleet. Wazuh on the Core is the MSP’s.
glossary.verify job: The backup server re-reading a backup, chunk by chunk, to confirm it is restorable before anyone needs it.
glossary.SLO: Service Level Objective — the availability you promise a client, as a number. The SLA is the contract around it.
glossary.SCA: Security Configuration Assessment — checking a machine's settings against a hardening benchmark.
glossary.Rules of Engagement: The written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.RoE: Rules of Engagement — the written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.triage: Quickly sorting alerts into real vs noise and deciding what to escalate — like an ER nurse.
glossary.baseline: A record of what 'normal' looks like, so you can spot what's abnormal later.
glossary.chain of custody: A documented trail of who handled each piece of evidence and when — so it holds up as proof.
glossary.agent: A small program installed on each machine that ships its logs to the SOC.
glossary.gate: A checkpoint at the end of a week — finish its required work before the next week unlocks.
glossary.eve.json: The file where Suricata writes its network alerts.
glossary.subnet: A slice of a network sharing an address range, e.g. 10.10.100.x.
glossary.Wazuh: The free, open-source SIEM/SOC platform this lab is built on.
glossary.Suricata: An open-source network intrusion detector that watches traffic and raises alerts.
glossary.Sysmon: A Windows tool that records detailed activity — processes, connections, file changes.
glossary.DVWA: Damn Vulnerable Web App — a deliberately insecure web app used as a safe attack target.
glossary.nmap: A scanner that finds open ports and what software is running on them.
glossary.nikto: A scanner that checks a web server for known issues.
glossary.MITRE ATT&CK: A public catalogue of attacker techniques, used to describe how an attack was carried out.
glossary.MTTD: Mean Time To Detect — the average time from an attack starting to it being noticed.
glossary.MTTR: Mean Time To Respond — the average time from detecting an attack to containing it.
glossary.rule.level: Wazuh scores every alert 0–15 by severity; searching rule.level:>=7 keeps the ones that usually matter.
glossary.rule.groups: The category tags Wazuh puts on an alert (e.g. authentication_failed, ids, web) — handy for filtering by attack type.
glossary.agent.name: The Wazuh field naming which machine an alert came from (e.g. Team07-ubuntu) — use it to filter to one host.
glossary.event channel: A named Windows log stream — Sysmon writes to Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational, which the agent forwards.
glossary.Emerging Threats ruleset: The community alert rules Suricata downloads with suricata-update — without them it sees traffic but raises nothing.
glossary.DQL: Dashboard Query Language — the field:value search syntax in the Wazuh/OpenSearch search bar (e.g. data.src_ip:10.10.30.7).
glossary.Discover: The Wazuh/OpenSearch view that lists raw events in a table you can search, add columns to, and save.
glossary.time picker: The date/time control (top-right) that sets which window of events you see — the #1 reason a correct search looks empty.
glossary.visualization: A saved chart (bar, pie, table) built from a search — the building block you drop onto a dashboard.
glossary.dashboard: A saved page of visualizations and searches you assemble to watch at a glance.
glossary.rule.description: The Wazuh field holding the human-readable name of the rule that fired — useful to group and count alerts by.
glossary.syscheck: Wazuh’s File Integrity Monitoring engine; its events carry syscheck.path and whether a file was added/modified/deleted.
glossary.sensor: A program on a machine that watches activity and reports it to the SOC — your Wazuh agent, Suricata and Sysmon are all sensors.
glossary.endpoint: Any individual computer on the network — a laptop, server or VM — as opposed to the network gear between them.
glossary.telemetry: The stream of activity data a machine sends about itself — processes, logins, connections — that the SOC watches.
glossary.hash: A short fingerprint calculated from a file; change one byte and the fingerprint changes, so it proves the file was not tampered with.
glossary.hashing: Running a file through a formula to get its fixed-length fingerprint (its hash).
glossary.SHA-256: A widely trusted hashing method that turns any file into a 64-character fingerprint.
glossary.false positive: An alert that turned out to be harmless — the tool flagged something that was not actually an attack.
glossary.true positive: An alert that was real — the flagged activity really was malicious.
glossary.enroll: To register a machine with the SOC so its agent starts sending logs.
glossary.brute force: Guessing a password by automatically trying huge numbers of combinations until one works.
glossary.port scan: Probing a machine to list which network ports are open, to discover what services it is running.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell — a way to log in to and run commands on another machine over the network, from your terminal.
glossary.pivot: To follow a clue (like an IP or username) from one log into related events, tracing an attacker’s movements.
glossary.hardening: Making a machine harder to attack by closing unused services, fixing weak settings and applying updates.
glossary.containment: Stopping an attack from spreading — e.g. isolating the affected machine — once you have detected it.
glossary.vulnerability: A weakness in software or configuration that an attacker could exploit.
glossary.vuln: Short for vulnerability — a weakness an attacker could exploit.
glossary.firewall: A filter that allows or blocks network connections by rule, to keep unwanted traffic out.
glossary.ufw: Uncomplicated Firewall — the simple command-line firewall on Ubuntu (e.g. ufw allow 22).
glossary.VLAN: A virtual LAN — one physical switch split into separate networks. Ports in different VLANs cannot talk without something routing between them, which is the whole point.
glossary.trunk: A link between switches that carries several VLANs at once, tagging each frame with its VLAN id (802.1Q). The alternative is one cable per VLAN.
glossary.native VLAN: The one VLAN a trunk carries UNTAGGED. If the two ends disagree about which it is, traffic silently lands in the wrong network — the classic trunk fault.
glossary.SVI: Switched Virtual Interface — a VLAN’s gateway configured on the switch itself. A switch with SVIs routes between VLANs at wire speed; a switch without them needs a router.
glossary.router-on-a-stick: Inter-VLAN routing done by a router over a single trunk, with one subinterface per VLAN. What you build when the switch cannot route — same outcome, one link carrying all of it.
glossary.EtherChannel: Two or more physical links bundled into one logical link, so a cable can fail without an outage and the bandwidth adds up. LACP is the protocol that negotiates it.
glossary.spanning tree: The protocol that stops a loop when switches have more than one path between them, by blocking all but one. It always picks a root switch — set it deliberately or it picks the oldest one.
glossary.PortFast: Tells spanning tree an access port has a PC on it, not a switch, so it forwards immediately instead of waiting. Never on a port that could reach another switch.
glossary.BPDU Guard: Shuts a PortFast port the moment it hears spanning-tree messages — which means somebody plugged a switch into a desk port. The protection that makes PortFast safe.
glossary.OSPF: A routing protocol: routers tell each other which networks they can reach, so each works out its own routes. It replaces static routes and reacts when a link dies.
glossary.OSPF area: A grouping that limits how far routing detail spreads. This course uses a single area 0 — the backbone — because one correctly adjacent area is the CCNA outcome.
glossary.adjacency: Two OSPF routers that have agreed to exchange routes. It has to reach the FULL state; anything less is the protocol telling you what does not match.
glossary.NAT: Network Address Translation — rewriting addresses as traffic crosses the edge, so internal addresses that mean nothing on the internet can still reach it.
glossary.PAT: Port Address Translation, sometimes "NAT overload" — the whole company sharing one public address, told apart by port number. What almost every small site actually runs.
glossary.ACL: Access Control List — an ordered list of permit and deny rules applied to an interface in one direction. It ends with an implicit deny, which is why the order matters.
glossary.port security: Limits which or how many MAC addresses a switch port accepts, so a stranger plugging into a desk port cannot quietly join the network.
glossary.ip helper-address: Tells a router to forward DHCP requests from a VLAN to a DHCP server somewhere else. The enterprise pattern, versus the router serving DHCP itself.
glossary.SNMP: The protocol a monitoring system uses to read a device’s interfaces, CPU and memory. Read-only is all a NOC needs; v3 is the version with real authentication.
glossary.syslog: Device log messages sent to a central collector. With synchronised clocks it turns "it broke this morning" into a readable sequence across every device.
glossary.NetBox: The source of truth for the network: sites, devices, interfaces, cables, VLANs and prefixes, with an API. It replaces the spreadsheet once the spreadsheet stops scaling.
glossary.Oxidized: Collects every device’s configuration on a schedule and commits it to Git, so you have both a backup and a history of what changed.
glossary.source of truth: The one system that DEFINES what the network should be. Tools read from it and configure devices to match, so the documentation cannot drift from reality.
glossary.PoE: Power over Ethernet — the switch powering the device on the far end of the cable, which is how phones and access points run without a plug of their own.
glossary.SFP: The slot a fibre (or copper) transceiver plugs into, for uplinks that go further or faster than the built-in ports.

red.blurb: You’re the ethical attacker — you find and prove the weaknesses before a real attacker does.
red.arc: Wk1 recon → Wk2 scan for weaknesses → Wk3 exploit with proof → Wk4 write up findings.
red.handsOffTo: GRC (your findings) and Blue (your attack evidence)
red.waitsOnFrom: GRC (the signed scope that authorizes testing)

blue.blurb: You’re the defender — you harden the systems, watch for the attack, and respond when it happens.
blue.arc: Wk1 harden the hosts → Wk2 set up monitoring → Wk3 detect & contain the attack → Wk4 report the incident.
blue.handsOffTo: GRC (what you hardened and the incident write-up)
blue.waitsOnFrom: GRC (the hardening standard) and Red (the attack to detect)

grc.blurb: You’re governance — you set the rules, score the risk, and turn everyone’s work into the reports.
grc.arc: Wk1 scope & asset inventory → Wk2 risk register → Wk3 policy & response plan → Wk4 final report & briefing.
grc.handsOffTo: Red & Blue (scope, standards) and leadership (the final report)
